claims.text: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a large caloric response under applied magnetic or pressure fields.
The untreated alloy tends to crack and has poor mechanical integrity or low compressive strength.
Pack cementation at approximately 950 °C for 24 h can introduce a thin silicide coating on the target alloy.
The coating will have a dual-layer structure consisting of an outer MSi2 layer and an inner MSi layer.
Oxide particles will form within emerging cracks in the silicide coating and produce self-healing.
The silicide coating will act as a mechanically robust crack-bridging layer.
During thermal and mechanical cycling, in situ oxidation products analogous to (Zr,Hf)O2 in HfNbTaTiZr will fill minor coating cracks.
Filling cracks with oxidation products will arrest crack propagation.
A sufficiently thin coating will minimally interfere with the phase transformations responsible for the caloric response.
The coating will increase compressive strength by an estimated factor of 2–3 relative to the uncoated alloy.
The coating will reduce caloric-performance metrics by less than 10% relative to the uncoated alloy.
The intervention is intended to remain effective during applied-field, pressure, and temperature cycling within a regime that preserves the intended phase transformation.
The intervention does not introduce rare-earth elements.
The coating may alter surface energy or stress distribution and thereby influence transformation kinetics.
A controlled comparison of coated and uncoated samples under identical field, pressure, temperature, and cyclic-loading conditions can test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain at least a twofold compressive-strength increase, or a caloric-response reduction greater than 10%, will falsify the hypothesis.
